articles.title: AI regulation rather than ban is better option: CJI
articles.excerpt:
Setting out clear rules to regulate usage of AI tools rather than a total embargo would be the right option for legal students and profession, said Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant.
Delivering the inaugural address at the first annual international conference on legal education convened by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association here on Saturday (November 21), the CJI observed that generative artificial intelligence had unsettled the assumption that an answer sheet reflects the knowledge of a student. Assessment methods should also be improved so that written works were supported by oral explanations. Ultimately, a law school must be able to certify with confidence what the students they had produced had learnt, the CJI said.
Referring to legal education in the country, the CJI noted that practical training can strengthen the doctrinal teaching only if it was genuine. A student learns strength of law in supervised mock trail than in examination. Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, the CJI said. Such clinical teaching requires trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards.
Justice P.S. Narasimha of the Supreme Court said students developed their legal reasoning through repeated draftings of petitions, analysing facts and finding out legal solutions on their own. Depending on AI tools for legal solutions without undergoing these rigorous training of draftings and legal reasonings, the students might lose the capacity to analyse and fail to distinguish between the right and the wrong, he said.
Attorney General R. Venkataramani said legal education to respond to the challenges brought about by the globalisation, technology and artificial intelligence. The law schools should evolve into centres of research and innovation while AI tools should be used to assist them. The AI should not be the master but an assistant, the AG said.
Acting Chief Justice of Telangana High Court P. Sam Koshy said it was high time everyone examined if next generation legal professionals were being prepared to merely understand what the law as it existed or equipping them to shape the laws the future demands. The present legal professional cannot be confined to legal framework of one jurisdiction. While learning a domestic law governing a dispute, one should also be aware of its international dimensions.
The Acting CJ said the future of Commonwealth’s legal tradition will not be secured by merely preserving its past. It can be secured by its capacity to learn, adapt and evolve without losing its foundational principles.
